purpose: Benazepril is used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension). Lowering your blood pressure helps protect your heart, kidneys, and blood vessels from damage. It may also be used to help protect your kidneys if you have diabetes or kidney disease.
how_it_works: Your body makes a chemical called angiotensin II that causes your blood vessels to tighten and your blood pressure to go up. Benazepril blocks the enzyme that makes this chemical, so your blood vessels relax and widen. This makes it easier for your heart to pump blood and brings your blood pressure down to a healthier level.
common_side_effects: The most common side effect is a dry, nagging cough that does not go away — this happens in some people and is not dangerous, but let your doctor know if it bothers you. You may also notice dizziness, especially when you stand up quickly, mild headache, or feeling a little tired. Some people notice a slight increase in potassium levels in their blood.
warnings: Do NOT take this medication if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant — it can seriously harm an unborn baby. Stop taking it and call your doctor right away if you notice swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat, as this can be a rare but serious allergic reaction called angioedema. Avoid potassium supplements or salt substitutes containing potassium unless your doctor says it is okay. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, especially blood pressure drugs, water pills (diuretics), or NSAIDs like ibuprofen.
typical_dosing: Most adults start with 10 mg taken by mouth once a day. Your doctor may gradually increase the dose to 20–40 mg per day, taken either once a day or split into two doses. Try to take it at the same time each day, with or without food. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but skip it if it is almost time for your next dose. Never double up.
